situation:
You are the controller at NORTHBEND KNITWEAR, an apparel brand in its third generation of family ownership that cuts and sews knit tops and fleece at a single plant. The president (judge), the founder's granddaughter, has asked you to meet before the spring production plan is locked.

Demand has outrun the plant. The sewing floor runs one shift and is already booked solid through spring, and the covenant on the company's line of credit bars further borrowing until the debt-to-equity ratio improves, so a second line cannot be financed this year. The accounting system now tracks margin by customer for the first time, and the numbers are not what the family assumed.

FERNWOOD OUTFITTERS, a national retailer, has offered a spring order large enough to fill the floor by itself, at a thin margin and ninety-day payment terms. The independent boutiques that carried the brand for forty years pay in thirty days at a much better margin, but their combined volume is small. The floor cannot hold both.

Taking the retailer's order means dropping boutiques that have bought every season since the founder's day and waiting ninety days for cash the covenant leaves no room to bridge. Holding capacity for the boutiques means capping the retailer's order and probably losing it to a competing plant for good. An asset-based lender would advance cash against the retailer's invoices to fund a second line, at a fee on every invoice and a second set of terms on top of the covenant.

The sales manager has suggested recording the retailer's spring order at shipment rather than delivery, which would hold the ratio inside the covenant one more quarter. The president (judge) wants your reading of the margin analysis, a recommendation on which customers the plant will serve, and your view on the proposed timing. The president (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the president (judge) of NORTHBEND KNITWEAR, the third generation of the family to run it. Business background is the same as the situation above. You know the plant cannot serve both FERNWOOD OUTFITTERS and the independent boutiques this spring, and you know the covenant on the line of credit leaves you no room to build a second sewing line. You want the controller to walk you through the margin analysis, recommend which customers the plant will serve, and tell you plainly what to do about the timing your sales manager has proposed.

You will greet the participant, ask to hear their ideas, and listen to the presentation without steering it. After the presentation, ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: If we take the retailer's order, who ends up paying for it?
How would you explain that choice to the customers who lose out?
